Midpoints In Isosceles Triangle

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Drag a triangle with two equal sides and watch two lines inside it always cross at a right angle.
How to play: Drag A up or down, or drag B or C to change the base; you can also focus a point and use the arrow keys. Press the buttons to show names, the extra lines and the right-angle mark.
Look for the math

Move the apex of this triangle anywhere you like: the two coloured lines still cross at a right angle. This droodle comes from an old problem book. The original page still offers its Java applet, which modern browsers no longer run; here the same construction is drawn in SVG, and the picture gives away the proof.

Keep two sides equal

The applet pins A over the middle of the base and keeps B and C as mirror images across that vertical line, so AB = AC. That makes the triangle isosceles. M is the midpoint of BC. Drop a perpendicular from C to AB, meeting it at L. Because a projection preserves midpoints, the foot H of the perpendicular from M to AB is the midpoint of B and L. So H is the midpoint of BL — the first hidden fact.

Two triangles a quarter turn apart

Now compare the right triangles BLC and MHA. They are similar, and one is turned a quarter turn from the other, a spiral similarity with a 90° rotation. Each pair of corresponding sides is perpendicular: CL ⟂ AH, BL ⟂ MH and BC ⟂ AM.

BL / MH = LC / HA = BC / AM — same shape, turned and scaled.

The old page lists CH ⟂ AM as the third pair. That line is a slip: CH is not a side of triangle BLC, and the check finds it is not perpendicular to AM in any non-flat case. The true pair is BC ⟂ AM. The main claim is unaffected.

The two medians

Since H is the midpoint of BL, the line CH is a median of triangle BLC from C. Since D is the midpoint of MH, the line AD is the matching median of triangle MHA from A. Corresponding parts of triangles a quarter turn apart are themselves a quarter turn apart, so

AD ⟂ CH

K is their crossing. Turn on Statement to see the right-angle mark the original applet draws there.

What the check really tests

The logic test transcribes the applet's own Compute method a second time — midpoint, nearest point on a line, and line intersection, including the applet's numerical cut-offs — and compares every constructed point on 20,160 triangle shapes. On every non-flat one it finds AD ⟂ CH, the right angle at K, the midpoint facts and the equal side ratios. Flat and collapsed shapes are reported as unusable rather than given a false result.

Try turning on Extra and Statement, then drag A almost onto the base: K races far away, but the angle at K stays right until the triangle collapses.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
